label: Classification and types
use_when: The subject is a family with several kinds, such as isolation levels, index types, garbage collectors, or caching directives, and the reader wants to know which kinds exist and what sets each one apart.
topic: The family itself, named as one noun phrase: the set of kinds the article classifies. Not a question and not a recommendation of one kind.
thesis: One declarative sentence claiming that a single criterion explains how the kinds differ: a claim a competent engineer would want justified. 'There are N kinds' is not a thesis.
focus_points: Three or more items: first the classification criterion, then one item per kind (two or more kinds). Each kind item names the kind and its defining trait under that criterion.
outline_rules: no_invented_problem: Do not invent a failure, incident, or problem scenario to motivate the subject. The article explains the family itself.
same_axis: Describe every type on the criterion from the criteria region, with the same points in the same order, so that the types can be read side by side.
no_ranking: Do not rank the types or recommend one. State what each type is and the condition under which its defining trait applies.
one_running_example: Choose one concrete case (one query, one request, one workload) and show how each type treats it in that region's example.
review_rules: weak_relevance: Remove a type region if the criterion does not set it apart from another type, i.e., it would get the same description as a type already covered.
write_rules: no_invented_problem: Do not open with or build toward a failure story. Motivate the article by what the reader will be able to tell apart after reading it.
same_axis: Give every type section the same internal order of points, so a reader can compare them without rereading.
no_ranking: Do not rank the types, list pros and cons, or recommend one. Say what each type is and when its defining trait applies.
one_running_example: Show the same concrete case under each type instead of a different example per section.

regions.outline: key_sentence defines the family in one sentence: what its members have in common and what they are for. elaboration names the types the article covers and the point of view it takes (core_message).
regions.write: Open with two or three sentences that define the family and state the article's point of view (core_message). Then name the types in the order they are covered, introduce the running case, and end with the question the rest of the article answers.

regions.outline: The criterion that divides the family. key_sentence states the criterion. elaboration explains what it measures and why it, rather than a surface difference, is what separates the types. example shows the running case and the question the criterion asks of it.
regions.write: Explain the criterion and what it measures before any type is described, and show the running case the later sections will reuse.

regions.outline: One type. heading names the type. key_sentence states its defining trait under the criterion. elaboration gives how it behaves and the condition under which that trait applies. example shows how this type treats the running case.
regions.write: State the type's defining trait under the criterion, explain how it behaves, and show the running case under this type with code, a trace, or a text diagram.

regions.outline: The whole family. key_sentence restates core_message in light of the types. elaboration says how the criterion orders the types relative to one another.
regions.write: Place the types side by side on the criterion in a few sentences and restate core_message in that light. Close with a short list of questions the reader should now be able to answer. Add no new claim. The heading names what the criterion explains, not 'Conclusion' alone.
